key_points.point: The document highlights that GenAI models improve over time by utilizing user prompts as training data, which providers leverage to enhance their systems. This mechanism of continuous learning is presented as a core feature of GenAI development, though it creates significant data privacy and confidentiality risks for users. From an accelerationist perspective, this feedback loop is essential for the rapid scaling of capabilities and the refinement of foundational models. The document notes that while some enterprise versions allow for data isolation, the default behavior of many platforms is to integrate user inputs into the broader training corpus.
key_points.verbatim: One of the most exciting aspects of GenAI is that the models can improve over time; however, this leads to various issues relating to the usage and ownership of inputs (i.e., user prompts). Various free and paid GenAI tools explicitly state that inputs may be used to train the platformÆs creation model.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Leverage user prompts as training data to accelerate the continuous improvement of generative AI models.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that prioritizes the integration of user-generated inputs into model training pipelines to facilitate iterative capability scaling. Encompasses: continuous model improvement, training data acquisition, feedback loop optimization.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes that users must exercise caution because GenAI providers often disclaim liability for inaccurate or harmful outputs, placing the burden of verification on the user. The authors argue that human review is a necessary safety mechanism to mitigate the risks of hallucinations or IP infringement. From a safetyist perspective, this highlights the inadequacy of current contractual frameworks to protect users from the systemic risks posed by AI-generated content. The document notes that providers frequently require users to indemnify them, further shifting the legal risk away from the developers.
key_points.verbatim: Most EULAs also encourage users to independently evaluate the outputs, through human review, before relying on it.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Mandate human review of AI outputs to mitigate risks of inaccuracy and harmful content.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that requires human-in-the-loop verification of AI-generated outputs to mitigate risks of inaccuracy and potential liability. Encompasses: human review, risk mitigation, liability shifting.

key_points.point: The document observes that EULAs are often structured to protect the provider, frequently disclaiming warranties and shifting liability to the user for any IP or privacy violations. This creates a power asymmetry where users are responsible for outputs they do not fully understand or control. From a skeptic perspective, this confirms that vendors use licensing agreements to insulate themselves from the consequences of their systems' failures. The document acknowledges that these terms vary significantly between free and enterprise versions, further complicating the user's ability to assess risk.
key_points.verbatim: Further, most EULAs contain provisions that favor and protect the provider. For example, CohereÆs indemnification requires the user to ôdefend, indemnify and hold harmless the Cohere parties from and against any claims, causes of action, demands, recoveries, losses, damages, fines, penalties or other costs or expensesö arising from or in connection with use of their GenAI platform.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Vendor EULAs are designed to shift liability to users and protect providers from accountability for AI-generated harms.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that vendor licensing agreements are structured to systematically shift liability and legal risk from AI developers to end users. Encompasses: indemnification clauses, liability disclaimers, power asymmetry.

factual_claims.claim: The Federal Circuit ruled that only human beings, and not AI systems, may qualify as an inventor under U.S. patent law.
The U.S. Copyright Office issued guidance stating that AI-generated material is not protectable when a human solely provided a prompt.
